data.hook: A simple table tallies 531 congressional hearings on major scandals, from Russia Hoax to Biden family issues—all with zero arrests. It strikes a chord, leaving many wondering why no one faces consequences.
data.name: Graphic Lists Hundreds of Hearings with Zero Arrests
data.summary: The graphic covers 15 topics like Covid with 82 hearings, Epstein files at 78, and January 6 at 106, boldly showing no arrests in any case. Replies express frustration over a perceived lack of accountability, with some blaming it for low voter turnout and midterm losses. While hearings focus on oversight rather than charges, rare exceptions like Steve Bannon and Peter Navarro's contempt convictions highlight how enforcement often stalls at the Justice Department. The image taps into widespread skepticism about Washington delivering real results.

data.hook: A map of ancient tribal invasions sparked talk of Rome's real downfall: a corrupt Senate more loyal to itself than the empire it served.
data.name: Roman Senate Corruption Parallels Draw U.S. Modern Debate
data.summary: The post argues the late Roman Senate's self-dealing and power grabs weakened the empire from within, much like today's U.S. senators accused of gridlock on election laws and voter rolls. Policy analyst Rachel Bovard explained current issues like top-down leadership, oversized committees, and a habit of needing 60 votes before acting, which sidesteps the chamber's design for negotiation. Users suggested fixes like repealing the 17th Amendment to make senators answer to states, while historians note how Roman bribery eroded effectiveness before invasions hit.

data.hook: Democrats claimed a strong win in the 2026 midterms, taking the Senate 56-44 and House 258-173. That result quickly led to heated online talks about how racial and ethnic groups vote.
data.name: Democrats Flip Senate and House in 2026 Midterms, Sparking Voting Pattern Debates
data.summary: Hypothetical maps showed every state blue if only Black voters participated, based on breakdowns of the electorate: 73% White, 9% Black, 10% Hispanic or Latino, 4% Asian, and 5% other. Conservative voices like Megan Basham argued high immigration from Hispanic communities has made the country more Democratic overall, despite past hopes for a conservative shift. Critics called these views racist, while Pew surveys confirmed wide Democratic leans among non-White groups, though some noted GOP gains in 2024 and individual variations within demographics.

data.name: Trump Blames Democrats for Market Drop and Iran Aggression After Midterms

Critics noted Republicans still hold power until January and pointed to other factors like AI stock worries, while supporters saw it as markets pricing in policy shifts.

data.hook: Harry Enten broke down the numbers on CNN, revealing Democrats' net favorability at -6 points after their 2026 midterm wins—a sharp drop from past wave years.
data.name: Democrats' Post-Midterm Polling Shows Weak Favorability Despite Gains
data.summary: Enten's analysis compared the current -6 favorability to +26 in 2006 and +3 in 2018, calling the results a vote against Republicans rather than a Democratic mandate. Leaders like Hakeem Jeffries (-17) and Chuck Schumer (-30) also polled poorly. A Pew survey found 67% of Americans, including nearly half of Democrats, worried Congress will focus too much on investigating the Trump administration instead of priorities like the economy.

data.hook: Georgia's long-dominant rural lawmakers watched their influence fade as Metro Atlanta's growing suburbs delivered a Democratic wave to the state Capitol.
data.name: Metro Atlanta Reshapes Georgia Politics with Democratic Sweep
data.summary: Democrats won statewide offices in the November 2026 election, including the governor's race claimed by former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, and took a majority in the state House for the first time in over two decades. Republicans clung to a slim Senate majority, but population growth and diverse voters in Atlanta's urban core and suburbs flipped key districts on issues like education and public safety. The shift ends decades of rural sway, prompting cheers for representation by people over geography alongside worries about rural priorities and the state's budget surplus.

data.hook: Voters who backed Democrats on affordability promises now question plans for higher taxes amid stories of soaring property bills.
data.name: Democrats Face Backlash Over Plans to Reverse Trump Tax Cuts
data.summary: Democrats campaigned on easing costs for families but now plan to unwind Trump-era tax cuts and tariffs after taking Congress in January. Critics, including a Wall Street Journal piece and Townhall analysis, warn this could raise average household taxes by $1,800 to $3,000 yearly, hitting middle-income families hardest as credits expire. Online frustration builds with personal tales like a woman's 'insane' property tax bill up 25% or $2,500 annually, while opponents tie amnesty ideas to job competition and higher rents. Democrats counter with healthcare subsidies and trade adjustments for long-term relief, but the rhetoric-policy gap tests early trust.

data.hook: With a fresh 56-44 Senate majority in hand, Democrats face a pivotal choice: kill the filibuster now or build toward 60 seats later.
data.name: Democrats Debate Scrapping Senate Filibuster After 56-44 Win
data.summary: Voices like Josh Marshall argue the filibuster erodes trust in democracy by blocking voter-backed laws and empowering the executive and courts, urging its elimination in January to act on the mandate. Neera Tanden counters that Democrats should aim for a filibuster-proof majority in 2028, warning that abolishing it risks letting President Trump push measures like the SAVE Act with his veto power intact. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed backs forward-looking leadership, endorsing Chris Van Hollen over Chuck Schumer, while talks swirl around reforms like a talking filibuster. The leadership fight and rules decision will define what this majority achieves before 2028.

data.hook: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis didn't hold back, labeling both Democrats and Republicans' handling of healthcare as 'political malpractice.' His words landed amid talks of rebranding Medicare for All as 'TrumpCare' to push it through.
data.name: DeSantis Calls U.S. Healthcare 'Political Malpractice' Across Parties
data.summary: DeSantis accused Democrats of wrecking the individual insurance market and Republicans of sticking to the status quo without real fixes. Minnesota Senator-Elect Peggy Flanagan said Democrats would back Medicare for All if called 'TrumpCare' to get it passed. An infographic highlighted the U.S. as the only wealthy nation without universal healthcare, with other countries like the UK in 1948 and Japan in 1961 achieving it decades ago, alongside worse U.S. outcomes like higher medical bankruptcies and lower life expectancy of 79.8 years. Online reactions urged action beyond slogans, from market reforms to addressing single-payer costs and wait times.

data.hook: A single repost from President Trump lit up online chatter about whether incoming Sen. Abdul El-Sayed has already outpaced Chuck Schumer's decades in office.
data.name: El-Sayed's Trump Repost Sparks Debate Over Schumer's Record
data.summary: Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who won Michigan's Senate seat in the 2026 midterms as the first Muslim senator, posted mock 'TrumpCare' images pushing Medicare for All. Trump reposted it without comment, prompting claims that El-Sayed has achieved more than Schumer's 27 years, including laws like the Inflation Reduction Act that cut drug prices and boosted clean energy. Critics call it mere posturing over real results, while supporters see savvy outreach in a divided Congress. The back-and-forth highlights Democratic tensions on strategy, bold moves, and what truly counts as power.
